_comment: seccomp-bpf profile for the Bayora model-gateway container.
WHAT THIS IS: a DEFAULT-ALLOW profile with an explicit DENYLIST of the
syscalls that would let a process escape or subvert its sandbox. It is a
reduce-the-attack-surface measure, not a sandbox.
WHAT THIS IS NOT: this is NOT a complete sandbox and it does NOT, on its
own, prevent a determined attacker from compromising the container. A
denylist can only block the syscalls it names; a new or unlisted syscall
is allowed by default. A sufficiently powerful syscall that is not on the
list (or a kernel-level exploit) can still break out.
STRONGER CONTROL: running the model-gateway under gVisor (runsc) provides
a user-space kernel that intercepts every syscall, rather than filtering
a list. Where gVisor is available it is the stronger control and should
be preferred. This profile is the fallback for hosts that cannot run
gVisor.
STATUS IN THIS REPOSITORY: configured_untested. This file was authored
and reviewed by hand, but no container was run under it in the authoring
environment (no container runtime was available), so its runtime effect
on the image's actual syscall trace is unverified. Before enabling it in
a deployment, run a regression test: start the gateway under the
profile, send one generation request through it, and confirm the
request completes and the service stays healthy.
WHY SOME ENTRIES RETURN ENOSYS INSTEAD OF EPERM: glibc's pthread_create
uses clone3 when the kernel offers it and only falls back to clone when
clone3 fails with ENOSYS. Denying clone3 with EPERM would therefore
break thread creation outright rather than force the fallback. The
clone3 entry is kept separate from the rest of the denylist for that
reason.
NETWORK SYSCALLS: the network group is ALLOW, not DENY. The gateway has
to reach the model server, and the containment of that traffic comes from
the Docker network namespaces (bayora-model-link and bayora-eval-net are
internal), not from seccomp. Denying socket() here would break the
service rather than harden it.
USAGE: apply it explicitly when the service is started.
docker run --security-opt seccomp=security/seccomp/bayora-model-gateway.json ...
For Compose, add under the service:
security_opt:
- no-new-privileges:true
- seccomp=./security/seccomp/bayora-model-gateway.json
The path is relative to the project directory when Compose resolves it.
SCHEMA: `architectures` is the OCI/runtime-spec spelling and `archMap` is
the older libseccomp spelling. Both are present so that the profile
loads on old and new runtimes; a runtime that does not recognise one of
the keys ignores it.

syscalls.comment: Sandbox-escape, kernel-observation and privilege-change primitives. Denied with EPERM so the caller sees a normal error rather than a crash. None of these are used by CPython, uvicorn or httpx.
clone3 is denied separately and with ENOSYS (38) rather than EPERM: glibc's pthread_create only falls back to clone() when clone3 fails with ENOSYS, so EPERM here would break threading entirely.

Network syscalls are allowed: the gateway must reach the model server. Containment comes from the Docker network namespaces (every network this service sits on is internal), NOT from seccomp. Listed explicitly so that the allowance is auditable rather than implicit.

The syscall set the CPython runtime, uvicorn and httpx actually depend on. Listed so that a future tightening of this profile has an explicit baseline to work from, and so that a regression test failure is easy to trace.
